newsitem.title: COMOROS: Secessionists urge Comoros islanders to stand firm.
newsitem.headline: Secessionists urge Comoros islanders to stand firm.

text.p: Secessionist leaders on the Comoran island of Anjouan have called on the islanders to stand firm against any moves by the government to restore its control there, residents said on Sunday.
Journalists on Anjouan reported that a small number of Comoros troops landed there early on Saturday.
Foundi Abdallah Ibrahim, 75, who leads the secessionist movement, was declared "president" of Anjouan by a crowd of islanders last week.
On Saturday, his bodyguards seized three government soldiers who they said had attempted to enter his residence, and paraded the soldiers before crowds of elated islanders.

Pierre Yere, an envoy sent by the Organisation of African Unity to investigate ways of ending the crisis, told Reuters on Saturday night that Comoros government leaders denied sending troops to Anjouan.

After meeting leaders of the Indian Ocean archipelago in the capital, Moroni, on Saturday, Yere was due to travel to Anjouan on Sunday to meet representatives of the islanders and assess the situation there.
Islanders on Anjouan, and on nearby Moheli, say they want to return to French rule because they have experienced nothing but poverty and political unrest since breaking away from France in 1975.

The poverty in the independent Islamic Republic of the Comoros contrasts with the comparative prosperity on the adjoining island of Mayotte, which voted against independence in 1975 and remains French.

Journalists on Anjouan reported on Saturday that a small number of soldiers landed there before dawn in an attempt to quell the secessionist protests. But there were no later reports of troop movements.

The secessionist leaders broadcast calls urging the islanders to gather in Mutsamudu, the island capital, and prepare for an invasion by Comoran government forces, islanders contacted by telephone said.
One islander said Anjouan was "awash with rumours" and the situation was tense.

The OAU said last week that envoy Yere, who comes from the Ivory Coast, would discuss measures to defuse tension "while addressing the legitimate concerns of the islanders while maintaining the unity, territorial integrity and cohesion" of Comoros.
On Moheli, a smaller island which also has a strong independence movement, demonstrators supporting Anjouan's secessionists set up road blocks.
France has refused to support the secessionists, saying the Anjouan situation is serious and could destabilise the whole region.
Three people including a gendarme were killed on July 14 as demonstrators, pressing for Anjouan to return to French rule or be independent, clashed with security forces.
